utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 3rd of June, 2009. Good afternoon, Mr. Pusic, Mr. Petkovic and Mr. Stojic, and good afternoon to you, Witness. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer and his associates, and let me also greet all the people assisting us. We are going to move to private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, I think you have something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. I was absent yesterday, although I did have a chance to look at the transcript. First, let me begin by thanking Mr. Stringer for his comments, and I appreciate those comments. Secondly, to the extent that my conduct contributed to the events that occurred after the hearing on last Thursday, I truly apologise. There was no intention on my part for things to escalate. Obviously, I will take full responsibility for the temperature in the room rising to the extent that some steam obviously was let off after the Judges left the Bench, and again I want to apologise both to the public but also to Mr. Stringer for any comments that I may have made that obviously caused the incident to occur. And if there is nothing further from -- I also understand that I'm being asked to provide further clarification as to other matters. I will do so. I believe the dead-line is set tomorrow. We are in the process of preparing a rather complicated motion that will be filed tomorrow, and given that, unless there's something else from the Bench, I would like to be excused for the rest of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, what you have just said has now been recorded, as we recorded yesterday Mr. Stringer's comments. You are right, yes, the temperature may rise, and it's important to make it drop. And I do invite everybody to cool down, which is far from being easy at times, the main thing being that international justice may prevail and unfold in the best climate possible in which everybody can express their views to defend their respective cases, be it the Prosecution or the Defence case. So this is what I wanted to convey to you. Besides this, Mr. Karnavas, your client, Mr. Prlic, is not in the courtroom, and please do forward to him our condolences because his father has passed away, unfortunately. That happened last week, and you know that we made everything possible for Mr. Prlic to be able to attend the funeral. Of course, some documents had to be obtained, which took some time, and he was able to fly on Saturday morning to attend his father's funeral. I think it took place on Sunday. So do convey to him all our condolences for this tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will do that, Mr. President. I did fail to mention that I did speak with Dr. Prlic earlier, and he wanted me to convey his gratitude and appreciation for everyone that was involved in making it possible for him to attend his father's funeral. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you asked whether you could be excused for the rest of the hearing. No problem. You decide whenever you want to attend or not. Inasmuch as you have a co-counsel, she can stay. We know that you have a lot of work. The two counsel don't have to be in the court all the time. Ms. Pinter, once again a very good afternoon to you. You may proceed for the remainder of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you very much. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General. Before we press on with our documents, there is something that we forgot to say yesterday. 3D02448, the e-court translation has been corrected in relation to Horvatincic Brigade. Can you now please go to document 3D01100, the Main Staff. We're still on the same binder, right, the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D01100, that document is to be found towards the end of the binder. There is no date. However, it refers to the period on or about the 30th of August. Binder number 1, Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have probably mislaid that one. I don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But you can look at the e-court copy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed my signature. The topic is the same, submit the written statement. I think we look --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, can the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. 3D0 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. There was some overlapping, and we did not get a translation or interpretation of the last answer from the general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my document. I signed it. The topic is the same. Over and over again, we unconditionally request that orders be carried out. This is the established practice in documents such as this one. Once you have to do a thing like this, take a step like this, it can only mean one thing: The structure is not what it should be, speaking of commander's responsibility. Disciplinary measures are always proposed, time and again, and you will see when we come to that, when we come to disciplinary measures and the police, we punished hundreds of people. And disciplinary measures were taken against hundreds of people who spent time in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Sir, 3D02758. General, please keep looking at the screen. This is binder number 1, Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document in front of me. It's my document. I signed it. This document talks about the fact that some HVO soldiers who, following the BH Army attack on Bugojno, failed to leave via Gornji Vakuf, rather they had to cross Serb-held territory, territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. Having spent some time in a camp or a prison somewhere, the Serbs allowed them to head for Zepce. It was convenient for them that the HVO was fighting the BH Army in Zepce and defending Zepce from the BH Army. This gave rise to the revolt of the part of those men's wives who at one point laid siege to the Main Staff. I, myself, was physically unable to leave the building because they wanted their men, their husbands back. For that reason, I here request that a list of those fighters from Zepce be forwarded to me, as well as their bills of health. The women's strike was a large-scale one, but then General Petkovic managed to deal with this in a peaceful manner, and this was something that he was better at than I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now please go to 3D03036. Again it's going to appear on your screen.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 31st of August. I relieve Vucica of duty. He was the commander of the professional battalion. Kresimir the IV was the name of that battalion. I here invoke the decree on the armed forces, although the question of legality of a document like this is open to challenge. Nevertheless, the reason for this was that it was no longer possible to work with this person. Could you now please call P03821, call up that document in e-court? It's not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, a technical question that should, by the way, have been asked of you a long time ago. I mean, there are so many questions to be asked, sometimes it's better not to ask anything because it can bring about further questions. Paragraph 1 of this order, it says it is the commander of a professional battalion. I'm somewhat surprised, because by definition, a military unit is a professional unit with soldiers, and here it's been stated as a professional battalion. Were there non-professional battalions? Why did you use the word "professional" in order to qualify this battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, as we've heard a dozen of times already, those brigades that went to the front-line were normally mobilised for a 10- or 15-day period, normally a battalion based on a brigade or more sometimes, and then it would go to the front-line. The entire composition or part of the brigade was outside of the mobilisation structure. They were at their homes, doing their jobs, working their land, performing farming tasks, and so on and so forth. And then several days before they were due to replace a battalion from the brigade occupying that position, they would be called up, and then they would go. They would leave their homes, bring along their own weapons, get on to lorries or buses, and then would be taken to those positions; whereas the remaining men would, in their turn, go home. That was how the HVO worked. At one point, we managed to set up some less professional units, which means that those men were available all the time. There were no breaks, two-week or fortnight-long breaks. They were either on the ground somewhere or put up in a house, in a building somewhere, or the Capljina barracks. Their pay was slightly higher. I'm not sure what it was exactly, but it was higher. Those were professional units. We referred to them as professional battalions, professional units, numbering 50 to 100 men or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now I understand your submissions better, what you said in your brief, where you said - and I shall return to the subject, trust me on that - you said that the HVO Army was not a real army. So through this example you have just provided, you say that there were, quote/unquote "soldiers" in the HVO that would till the land and who would at times be mobilised to go to the front-line, and then they would return home to carry on working. And then there were others, probably less of them, who were soldiers around the clock, as it were. Is that how the situation was in the HVO, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so, Your Honour, but there were always fewer of those. And those other people, in addition to working their land, were plying other kinds of trade, whatever they used to do in their civilian lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question that might be useful to all, including the Prosecution. In percentage, in your view, in the HVO, how many were the 100 percent professional soldiers and how many amateurish soldiers were there, so those who may be in uniform sometimes and then would return to their usual occupations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was there, speaking of professional soldiers, all together the number would be under 1.000, not even that many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over 1.000 out of how many all together, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 1.000, under 1.000. Receiving their salaries from the HVO were a total of 40.000 people, and then the BH Army, Tuzla, Posavina, all together, a total of that 40.000 men; Sarajevo, Bihac, everything that the HVO covered. Over a half of those men were under the command of the BH Army or about a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So now I'm keeping these important figures in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question, Mr. Praljak. What about the officers, the cadre, non-commissioned/commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation was very poor, Judge Trechsel. Surely you know that the commander is the linchpin. He is the center of the army, the backbone, if you like. We had few commanders, no command staff to speak of at any level. Over a total of the officers and NCOs that we had available to us, I think very few of them actually had received any formal military training whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we to understand that out of the 1.000 professional servicemen, there were about 100 officers and non-commissioned officers; is that how we should understand things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour, I think you misunderstand me. I was talking about the total of officers and NCOs throughout the HVO. In my opinion, or at least as far as I know, under 10 percent of those had received any sort of formal a military training. These thousand men, there is no way there would have been 100 NCOs there. Those were minor units with a single commander or two subsidiary ones. If there was a 40-man unit, there would be one commander. If it was a professional unit, such as the Bruno Busic unit, it was located in four or five different places. Its name was Bruno Busic. A minor element was in Central Bosnia, another element was located in the Capljina barracks, and so on and so forth. One can by no means speak of any sort of quality structure, not in the sense that there were platoon commanders, company commanders, and so on and so forth. Those were simply people who had some merits to their names. Normally, those were the bravest people, and the bravest ones became commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have not actually answered my question. It went to a professional -- professionality, not as far as quality, but as far as permanence is concerned. Would the commanders also go home for two weeks after two weeks in the field? You certainly did not. At what grades did the permanence stop? I hope I make myself understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fully, and now I can answer. At battalion level, he no longer -- he would go home with his men. It was the brigade commander that was permanent because there would always be a battalion somewhere on the ground. The brigade command was, let's say, fully employed, full-time employed. The battalion commander, for example, would go somewhere with his men and then go back home to deal with his own business until his battalions or companies were called up again, and then they would go back. There was no permanence in terms of how much time he was spending in the ranks. He would be there for a week or two as a soldier, and then the next two weeks he would go back to being a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. It's a pity that this sort of issue should be discussed three years down the track. If you have 1.000 professional soldiers in the HVO, not to mention the 39.000 men who would come and go, depending on their professional occupation, elsewhere, out of the 1.000 men how many were there who were former JNA officers who had undergone military training, like General Petkovic? How many were there who came from the former JNA who had been career officers? How many of them did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were 1.000 professionals. And among them, I don't really know. There were very few, next to no one. There was Mr. Dragan Curcic, who later became the number two man of the Federation's command. Speaking of this battalion mentioned here, there was no one there, very few. Your Honours, I could nearly count them all myself. Blaskic, Petkovic, Siljeg, the Canadian Army Glasnovic -- sorry? No, no. Obradovic. A total of under ten men occupying such positions, professionals from the former JNA. I'm talking about the total, between 10 and 15. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You see, once you tackle a topic, there are others that would ensue. One very last -- I could go on for hours, as you can imagine, but I'm discovering -- I'm not speaking about other people. I'm speaking on my own behalf. I now discover that within the military structure of the HVO, there's just a handful of JNA officers, very few of them. You've just given a few names: Siljeg, Blaskic, Petkovic, Obradovic, so maybe under ten men. If that was so, and I suppose it was, it may be that the Prosecutor is going to challenge that, but if it was speaking of the Republic of Croatia as part of the technical, quote/unquote, "technical support" provided by it, and I'm speaking in conditional terms here, noting that there is basically no officer within the military HVO, would it not have been normal for the Republic of Croatia to second HV officers in order to support and structure the HVO. You know countries that send officers in order to support armies that are just in the making elsewhere. Should that not have happened? And if it didn't happen, why didn't it happen that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As Your Honours have seen, I stopped some people. Someone would sometimes arrive, but not because the Croatian Army officially approved or okayed that. I used my own channels to get people seconded as volunteers, actually, not officially. Croatia had very few men, in relation to the overall number of soldiers, who were former JNA officers. The best part of those who were former JNA officers, most of those obviously did a splendid job, but some wanted to remain behind in their offices. Quite many of them refused to go out and fight with their units. Their reasoning was they should stay at the back and send trained men forward to attack. But the soldiers didn't like that, and they refused to put up with that, the simple reason being the Croatian Army at the time was to a large extent an army of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to put another question, because otherwise I could be reproached with not having tackled all the facets of the issue. I talked about the formed JNA officers in my questions, and you said there were less than ten men. But I have to add this now: Let us imagine that JNA officers became officers in the Republic of Croatia and that they are, therefore, officers of the Croatian Army. Let us imagine that later on they have their private motivations, and they decide to volunteer in the HVO. Therefore, they leave the Croatian Army to be volunteers in the HVO. As far as you know, how many officers of the Croatian Army -- how many became HVO officers? I'm talking about men who had been first JNA officers or officers in other armies; it's quite possible. How many of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, first of all this figure ten that I mentioned at first, I couldn't list more than ten of them. There may have been some others there, but whether it's 10 or 12, that's for the first piece of information. As for the second piece of information, well, I know almost all of them that we managed to win over; Petkovic came, I came, Akrap came, Poljak was there for a short while, Andabak was there for a short while. They stood in for me. Well, maybe ten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, could you quote the numbers slowly, please, because the court reporter cannot take down the names. Please give us the names of the officers in the Croatian Army that volunteered. You mentioned Praljak, Petkovic, Andabak. Who are the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Praljak, Petkovic, Andabak. There are several Andabaks, but he's from the Croatian Army, and he replaced me. He was there in 1992, but for a very short time. Then he was replaced by Poljak for a short time, Zeljko Akrap, Zeljko. Zeljko Akrap was there also. And then who else? In Central Bosnia, at one point I managed to get, in 1992, when I was up there trying to calm the situation down -- as people were saying, I managed to get four or five officers from Split using my own private channels. They agreed to go up there for us for just a few days to assist in structuring the HVO but also the BH Army. So they were there at their disposal, too, to teach those people about artillery and also to set up the books, the records. They were there for 25 days. Now -- well, Mr. Petkovic was there for the longest time. Others were there for brief periods of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter, I'm sorry to have taken up some of your time. It seemed important to me to look into these questions in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a note, Your Honour. I have to remind you, at the beginning of the trial I asked that, first of all, we should deal with the basic military issues and then we will all be able to understand the situation. Unfortunately, this trial does not allow us to do that, but you remember quite clearly this request on my part that this should be the starting point. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your questions never disturb or disrupt anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I have to tell you that the document that you have requested is prepared in the binder to be explained, which means that Judges would have to skip some documents. Let us move back to the Main Staff, to binder number 2, and in binder number 2 of the Main Staff we should go to document 3D00929. The date is the 11th of September, just to make it easier for everyone to find their way around.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this document is a report that was submitted to the VOS of the Main Staff, so that's the Main Staff, and it is signed by Raspudic. The document is comprehensive and exhaustive, and it describes the positions of the BH Army in the town of Mostar, the disposition, and I wouldn't have anything to add. But I would like to note that at page 2 of the Croatian text, at the very bottom of the page, there is a sentence which is very important because I have been talking about those things. And the sentence reads like this: "As far as the political climate on the left bank is concerned, our sources have told us that the people of Mostar, the locals, the local population, are in favour of the cessation of the hostilities of the war. They favour Mostar as an open city where they would live side by side, Croats side by side with Serbs and Muslims." And then it goes on to say -- well, I don't want to quote, but people who have come from other municipalities, Gacko, Nevesinje, advocate the policy of a Muslim Mostar all the way down to Zovnica, which is on the route to Siroki Brijeg. So here a man who received this information because he had some connections with East Mostar, I don't know what kind of connections, but he's saying what I have been saying over and over again. Unfortunately, the refugees were in such a mental state, expelled, in many cases many of them were killed, and they did not have any vision or any guarantee that they would go back to their homes; and history proved them right. For the most part, they did not go back to their homes, at least as far as Republika Srpska is concerned. And the international community failed them there, the UN failed them, all the declarations failed them. And they were looking for new areas to live, and by definition, you know what it means. And I claim that the conflict between Croats and Muslims would be much more difficult to cause, it would have less consequences, it would have been less severe, had there been no such major shifts in the ethnic composition. I called it the ethnic occupation. People - well, I fully under them - came in. They lost their family members, they lost their homes, and they are looking for a new place to live. And that's it, as far as this document is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to correct the transcript at page 16, line 9. The general said: "I fully understand these people," and that has not been recorded in this transcript in this manner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said, because I met those people, I saw those people, I found accommodation for those people, and those were desperate people who revert back to the instinct. Please do not misunderstand me; the animal force. They are just looking for a place to live, so I'm not being insulting here. These are the elementary forces, the instinctive forces, looking for a place to live. And, of course, this is engenders conflict with the area where they find themselves in because there are too many of them, far too many of them for this situation to be bearable. And nobody ever gave them any guarantees that they would be able to go back to their homes or give them any hope, and we all know what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we have to go back to the first page of this document, where it says where the Command of the unit in Mahala is located. This is a reference to the unit of what unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the sniper activities targeting Stotina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a lot of information in this text, but it is quite clear. I'm sorry for the interruption. Of course, all the commands were located among the people of Mostar. All the BH Army headquarters were located among the civilians: Brigade, battalion, and corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, it is not amiss to repeat it once again. 3D02578.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here Mr. Zarko Tole, a major general at the time, the 13th of September, asks for a passage to be allowed for Mr. Jakov Bienenfeld --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to revert back to the first document because I've discovered something which could be of interest. Seemingly, this report or document dates back to the 11th of September, 1993. The people who drafted this report never imagined that judges sitting in an international tribunal would have a look at these documents that contain some interesting information. I have the feeling that in addition to this document, there must have been a map on which 24 sites had been located, since on the last page of the caption that states that in such a place there was a bunker and so on. On looking at item 18, which gives us the position of a sniper, number 19, where another sniper is also positioned, and number 23, where a sniper is also positioned, these are snipers from the ABiH, I assume. It would have been interesting to see this map to position 18, 19, and 23, those numbers on the map, to plot them and see what the firing angle must have been. That was your job. If I had conducted an investigation, that's what I would have done, but maybe you didn't notice this. Do you understand me? At numbers 18 and 19, snipers have been positioned, based on the information provided, as well as on number 23.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, probably did not append the map because every man from Mostar knows exactly where the restaurant Petica is, where Jagnje is, where the RTV Service is. So he gave it -- well, this pertained to the command of this zone, Mostar, and every person in Mostar knows exactly the precise position. So there's no need to draw it. Well, I didn't think that this was -- well, the time is running out, and I could talk for 200 hours about every single topic in great detail, but unfortunately my time is running out. So I thought that this was quite clear. Of course, yes, there were snipers. And after all, Your Honours, in all BH Army positions where there were snipers targeting HVO soldiers, well, these were illegal soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, it took me just a few split seconds to realise this, since I am seeing the document for the first time. And I realised instantly that at items 18, 19, and 23, snipers have been positioned. Now, if you look at number 18, maybe you are able to give us an explanation. It says "7.9 millimetres," "Serbian 7.9 millimetres."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it means that the Serbs had a sniper rifle, 7.9 millimetre, and that's what he calls it. So this is not the position from which a sniper was being active. It's not the Republika Srpska Army position, but it is a reference to a sniper rifle manufactured in Kragujevac, in a Serbian factory. And that's why it was called the Serbian rifle, Serbian sniper, 7.9 millimetre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: "18. Position," we understand that a sniper is there on and off and that he uses 7.9-millimetre rifle. Either the sniper is there from time to time, and he belongs to the ABiH, and he is using a rifle, a Serbian rifle, or this is a soldier from the VRS who is a sniper and who is also firing. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here it is highly likely that a BH Army soldier is using a 7.9-millimetre sniper manufactured in -- yes, but I know for a fact that from Serb positions, positions held by the Republika Srpska Army, snipers did target Mostar. I know that from my own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, these positions on the map, it was for you to do this. You could have, perhaps, when you were conducting the cross-examination of the Prosecution witnesses, you could have demonstrated with this document the fact that the ABiH had positioned snipers in certain locations. And from there, they could fire at the victims that were mentioned on our list, but maybe you didn't think of that. You can't think of everything. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I want to insist on this question regarding the map. I must say that I find your answer in this respect absolutely unconvincing. If there is a legend with certain points, that there is no way of knowing what locality they refer to; number 18 and following are examples. No one can guess what that refers to, and no one writes such a legend if there is not a map attached to it. Your Defence brought this document. Where is the map? Where is that map, and why is it not here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, you are entirely right when it comes to this. Apparently, you misunderstood me. I said that I didn't have a map. We didn't have a map, but this -- these terms, Petica, Jagnje, and so on, everybody knows that in Mostar. Perhaps I misspoke, and I'm sorry for that. But it is true that a map was appended to it, to this document, but I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we looked through the archives, and a map was not appended to this document. You can see that this is a document that was taken from the archives, from the Croatian National Archive. And this map did not exist. Had it existed, it would have been appended to this document. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As my colleague has just said, I'm sure there was a map. If you look at number 9, it says the MOS members "sleep here," so the place where the MOS soldiers are sleeping have been identified. Item 10 mentions a bunker. Item 14 says there is a bunker inside the store. So all of this has been positioned or plotted on the map, and there must have been a map appended to this document. It's a shame we don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend, Ms. Alaburic, has drawn my attention to the fact that the buildings are at Santic Street. Santic Street was the confrontation line along which clashes were occurring in Mostar. All these positions are at Santic Street. We can make available to you a map of Mostar showing Santic Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, I don't know whether Mr. Ivica Raspudic, the author of this document, is still alive, but as part of your defence, you could have met him and told him, Well, we have this document which you have drafted. Together with a map I give you, could you plot points 1 to 24 on this map? This is something you could have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the trial entailed fewer documents, if there were fewer documents that we were dealing with. But given the amount of documents that we are facing, I admit we have not had enough time to deal with this, which doesn't mean that we will not find something before Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, 3D02578. 3D02578. The date is the 13th of -- you started talking about Bienenfeld?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about the map. Perhaps we could draw one. Nevertheless, along the entire confrontation line in Mostar, there were positions on either side of the confrontation line. That's why I did not consider that to be of any particular importance. We did mark a confrontation line. On either side of the line there were BH Army positions and HVO positions. What this is about is Mr. Jakov Bienenfeld. It is about this: Since the end of 1992, I think late November or early December that year, when Mr. Bienenfeld came to see me, his father was a retired JNA general, and he got actively involved again in the Croatian Army. He had a PhD in Chemistry. He was a specialist in chemistry. I didn't have quite enough time to introduce this. Some foreign jobs were given to him. And he had to go to Bijelo Polje to see if there were any chemical poisons being produced there, which during the former Yugoslavia were being sold to Saddam Hussein, but I'm not going into that now. Let's go back to his son. From the end of 1992 to October 1993 or thereabouts, Mr. Bienenfeld organised 10 or 11 convoys to Sarajevo and from Sarajevo. He brought medicine and food into Sarajevo. Those were Jewish organisations. Mr. Bienenfeld is a Croatian Jew. Jews were leaving Sarajevo on these convoys in order to not remain behind and be killed in Sarajevo, plus the women and children who managed to join the convoys. And then the Jewish heirloom was taken out, if I may call it that, items that had to do with their tradition and civilization. There were a total of 10 or 11 convoys, I think. All of those convoys were organised with the assistance of the HVO: Bruno Stojic, Petkovic. I had a role to play as well. Jakov Bienenfeld described my role in his -- in his statement to this Tribunal, which is available to the Chamber. He describes how that worked, what it was like, and what exactly happened. Our drivers went there. They drove across Serb-held territory. There were all sorts of unpleasant situations occurring. In the process, most of the technical aspects where taken care of by Zarko Keza from the Main Staff. He was a military officer in the Main Staff. That's as much as I can tell you about that. A total of 10 convoys were organised, and that is no mean feat. That is how I feel. If we had done no more than that, I think that would have been plenty to keep one busy throughout the time. The Chamber can refer to Jakov Bienenfeld's statement, which describes exactly my role.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, these humanitarian convoys drove into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part medicine and food, to the extent that they could and the amounts that they could manage. And they brought out people, human beings. We tried to save the Jews from the hell hole that was Sarajevo. If you take a historical perspective, they were the victims of the greatest sufferings. And one is naturally sensitive to that sort of thing, so we tried to give them a hand. It wasn't the Jews alone, however; women and children were on those convoys leaving Sarajevo, too. There were some problems with the Serbs. It's complicated. Let's just move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Can we please move on to P05079. The date is the 15th of September, 1993, the order to attack given by Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document. Nevertheless, I believe this has been exhibited already, or hasn't it? This is Arif Pasalic's order to carry out an attack that was part of the Neretva-93 operation. This was produced other 15th of September, 1993. And it's exactly who should go where and what they should do. Based on this master plan that Arif Pasalic produced, Sejtanic, being the commander of Sector South, drew up his zone plan to attack whom and Mostar and so on and so forth, so there you go. Will you please just -- can we please go back to Uzdol, 3D02415. No need, perhaps. Uzdol is something that we've done already. 3D02415. This is a report, or, rather, a brigade, after they committed the massacre in Uzdol on the 14th of September, killing 30 civilians and capturing some soldiers and so on and so forth. And then people simply asserted that we were entirely naive and insane. We were talking about coexistence, and people knew that there were weapons coming in and refugees being received. All the while, Mr. Izetbegovic was signing away, signing false declarations. That's what they believed, and that's what I believed. I just want to say that I was in the area on those days, and we launched a counter-offensive to prevent another massacre that would have been even worse. I want to say there were no acts of retaliation whatsoever. I and other people there made an enormous effort to keep anything like that from happening. We expended enormous amounts of energy. This was a village inhabited by a total of perhaps 150 people, yet 41 human beings were killed. This can only cause an enormous disruption to the mental setup of this entire area. Whoever never found themselves in a situation like that would probably find it impossible to understand, no amount or level of education and insight. Nevertheless, I wouldn't wish a thing like this upon anyone. I do think that the understanding is insufficient of how a war works, what suffering means, what misery means, what mental disturbances mean that can be brought about by war situations and so on and so form. Be that as it may, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. I think we should have gone through this document, nevertheless, because they're talking here about the axes of attack through Mostar and the siege.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sejtanic provides a very good description of this in his book. I think we've covered that ground before, and I don't think there's any point in --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. 3D0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is an order to attack, a very comprehensive document, several pages' long. And that goes into detail and seems to be a draft. You will have noticed that under item 17, no date or time is given. However, when it comes to the degree of detail, everything is mentioned and said, and I'm sure it did not escape your notice. Under item 6(d), it says that a signal for attack must be received. I'm also looking at this document for the first time, but I only need a few seconds to react. It doesn't take me hours to understand the scope or the extent of a document. If I apply this to the Mostar attack, in your case, you claim that the ABiH had planned a large-scale attack on the 9th of May. As is to be found here, there must have been a very detailed order to attack, but there could have been another draft or another plan, which was to attack a few locations, without going into detail. And it may be that there was a massive response by the HVO so that from the outside one could have been under the impression that it was an attack initiated by the HVO. So the Judges will have to look into all sorts of possibilities, based on the Prosecution evidence and your evidence. I have a very simple question. If, indeed, there was an ABiH attack on the 9th of May, should we find a similar order to this one at the level of the 4th Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe you misunderstand this. This attack occurred on the 15th of September, 1993. This is part of Neretva-93. The way a plan was drawn up for Sector South --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I understood that very well. I understood that this is an order from September. Then I have some kind of inductive method. I'm saying that if there was this kind of order in September, I wonder whether there was a similar order in May, prior to the 9th of May. That is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were orders just like this one by Mr. Pasalic and the commander of the 1st Mostar Brigade, from April 1993, orders to attack Mostar, with a large-scale map, with all the axes drawn in. I've used these in court, and I've demonstrated all of this with great degree of precision for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, all the axes of attack, where exactly they were attacking through the two by two-and-a-half metres map, all the axes, what the targets were, and how they meant to go about taking those targets. The attack took place on the 9th of September, 1993, or rather the 9th of May, 1993. The attack was carried out, and someone was watching from a hill top and arrived three hours later, so now they suddenly knew who had started the attack. This is erroneous information and false reports by people who misunderstood. Obviously, five or ten minutes after their attack, the shooting started there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall have a look at this famous map of the 1st Mostar Brigade of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have prepared something for the Trial Chamber in relation to all the admitted documents in relation to the BH Army, so you will have that in front of you so that you can see everything, the orders for attacks and all these other elements.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I was going to move on to 3D0308, the date being the 16th of September, 1993. That is your document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my document. The 16th of September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it perhaps the number 3D03038?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D03038.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. The contact between me and General Petkovic, who is -- Mr. Petkovic -- well, I have really no idea. We in Sarajevo, in central Sarajevo, wherever. I think it was Sarajevo. I got my approval for him to assume any of the form of authority necessary to start negotiations, especially as regarded the cessation of hostilities, which is what we were after, and to make sure that the interests of the Croatian population and the Croatian Republic of HB were best served. Nevertheless, this was at a time when the secret agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic was reached on the federation and the confederation with Croatia. Confederation with Croatia, that is one thing that no one seems to be keeping in mind, just as though it was never signed. On that same day, an agreement was signed between Alija Izetbegovic, Karadzic and everyone else, the famous agreement with the Serbs about cessation. There was a dual policy in terms of both politics and military policy being informed. There was a dual policy at work, a double strategy, if you like. They agreed on a partition with the Serbs. They said, Okay, there would be a referendum after a while. And they said the armies would no longer continue fighting, and yet at the same time -- or by this time for two months already, Sefer Halilovic and his army had been attacking the HVO. We can keep at this for another 500 years, and this will always be true. It will always be the only unambiguous truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 27, line 23, General Praljak was talking about a secret agreement on confederation with Croatia. What was recorded was a secret agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic. I don't know what exactly you said, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tudjman and Izetbegovic. I am sorry. They were the ones who signed the secret agreement whereby the Croats and the Muslims would share a state in Bosnia and Herzegovina, because Mr. Izetbegovic, by this time, had understood that he had nothing on the Serbs and that the international community would not give him a hand, in terms of beginning to be on an equal footing with the Serbs and being able to fight them. And then he signed this agreement on a federation with two components in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that this federation would become part of a confederation with the Republic of Croatia. On that same day, or thereabouts, he sat down with Karadzic and Milosevic and signed an agreement to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina into two parts in which the Muslims, as the agreement reads, would constitute a majority in one part. And then what was envisaged was that those two parts would be separated following a referendum. And the part containing the Muslim majority would remain an independent state, with all the implications that this had in terms of any international documents and agreements that were signed, the UN and so on and so forth, and the other part would then join Serbia. That's what it says. That's with the army. They stopped all the clashes immediately, and they turned on the HVO in their entirety in a bid to make up for the territory that had been lost. This was an act of aggression, a pure act of aggression, and nothing else. And it had been like that for at least three months. We can stay here for another 500 years and try to talk about this, but it will always stay what it is; an act of treason, an act of trickery, and a disingenuous policy that was being implemented. We made a huge effort to reach an agreement, to have a joint army, to remain on an equal footing. Each and all of us, we can say whatever we like, but my opinion is crystal clear. I have seen so many documents. There is no one who can change my opinion in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, what you've just said comes in support of your defence case. As far as you know, did Croatian political analysts or Bosnian political analysts share your view? Do they say that there was an agreement between Karadzic and Izetbegovic which would account for the fact that an attack was launched against you? Do politicians and political analysts write about this? Do we have any articles about it or is this the outcome of your thinking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, these are historical facts. This document was made public. It's a public document. That's not something that Praljak invented. It's a signed document, a public document. It's not a figment of Praljak's fantasy. You saw the text where the people from Rama say, We are naive fools. Well, every soldier down there knew that. People are smart, and if it's about their survival, they get even more smart. You can -- they see everything. You can see everything. Hundreds of texts have been written on this topic, but only -- well, those who wanted the talks to be resolved in this manner, people from the international community, the great powers who wanted that. Because of our problems in the information part, they were saying the HVO is attacking, the HVO is attacking. Well, we've seen hundreds of documents here. We did not attack anyone anywhere. Well, taking an elevation or a tactical point that I had lost before, yes; that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last follow-up question. Assuming what you see as a real fact, but as a Judge I've got to be cautious, I can only have assumptions that I put to witnesses that confirm or disagree with it. At this stage I am not supposed to have any opinion. So based on this assumption that you are telling the truth, in such a case there was a general attack against you, against the HVO, in full agreement with the Serbs. In taking this political and military risk, did Izetbegovic not run the risk of having the Republic of Croatia - it had, after all, military means - the risk of the Republic intervening, not in an underground way by financing this score of officers that came from its own ranks, but would have its brigade intervened to face the ABiH? Was there not such a possible military and political reaction coming from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. There was no such reaction for a very simple reason; because Izetbegovic knew full well that Croatia, in this [indiscernible], would be labelled an aggressor, the party that attacked Bosnia-Herzegovina, and nobody dared even dream of something like that. You'll see a document here - we'll exhibit it here today or tomorrow - that on the 24th, the day I arrived, I sent a request or a demand to Franjo Tudjman and to Gojko Susak for two battalions of the Croatian Army because there was an attack on Vakuf which was very fierce. Bugojno had already fallen. I didn't get anything. I asked for two battalions to cover the TG-2 line - this is what Judge Trechsel asked, what TG-2 was down there - for the HV to at least take that part and to -- so that I could get a certain number of people for other tasks. You will see where I am asking for two cannon barrels to be replaced. I'm asking Gojko Susak to arrange it in the repairs facility in Sibenik, and that was supposed to be financed by our people in Croatia who had contributed. Well, I am talking to him, cap in hand, asking for two cannon barrels and for 30 people. I don't know. There was an agreement signed between Muslims and Serbs. That was not a secret agreement. They made it public. And there are signatures, I think, of some major figures from the international communities, and what is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when you became aware of this, you asked for two battalions. They were not given to you. Did you then call your friend, Mr. Susak? Why didn't you call him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Between -- after the question, Mr. Praljak said, Yes -- no. He said, No, I think. But it was not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it had to do with something earlier, something that was said earlier. I wanted to comment. So I called Susak, and he told me quite clearly the same thing that I -- Your Honours, well, when I was in Croatia, and if I had been in Croatia, I would have presented the same position. At that time, Croatia was not in a position to give the troop, because it would be labelled an aggressor, and it would endanger its very survival. The international community was not in favour of having a Croatian state. The English were not in favour of that, neither were your French, Your Honour, and other people were not in favour of that for various historical reasons. But as an HVO commander, who is aware of the fact that he can lose the war, be defeated and to be routed, to be really well defeated; so I am asking for two battalions with a different hat on my head. And we will find the document and the TG-2. I didn't get anything. He told me, Praljak -- or, rather, he used my nickname. He didn't say "Praljak." He said, I can't give you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For this to be on the record, I'm asking you this: What did Mr. Susak tell you over the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me that I couldn't get it, that he can't give it to me, that he won't give it to me, and that if I could find some volunteers, that I could go. And then I asked, Well, there are some people from the 5th Brigade. So I used my private channels. There were maybe 50 or 60 people from the 1st Guards Brigade, 30 people from some other brigade, and so I called the commanders using my private channels, people I knew; and I begged and, Come on, man, get at least 30 or 40 people together so that you could cover some of the positions I have to hold because otherwise we will be routed. And that's how I managed to get the 130 people from the 5th Brigade, the 5th Guards Brigade. Those were fighters from Vukovar who had managed to break through the siege of Vukovar, and they joined and fought in this war, and maybe some hundred people from two other brigades that covered some position near Mostar at Hum and so on. Officially, I did not get anything, and officially I couldn't get anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have another ten minutes before the break, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would just like to tell the Trial Chamber -- you asked whether there were any documents pertaining to this agreement between Izetbegovic and Krajisnik. Well, there is a document. It's contained in 3D00320. That's a compendium of all the agreements between 1991 and the end of the war. When we started the Defence case, we went through this document, and the same document -- well, my colleague Ms. Alaburic helped me. It's under 5D1040 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who co-signed it, Ms. Pinter?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's signed by Krajisnik and Izetbegovic. And I have the pages here, but only in Croatian, not in English. But this is agreement 151. In the book, it will facilitate you finding that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the speakers please not overlap. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If I may just correct the number of the document. Page 34, line 3, the document number is 4D1040, if you want to look at it immediately, and it is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have this document. I haven't got it here with me, but it has, indeed, been tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's behind your back in the binder entitled "The Truth about Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we've discussed this document. This document, which is 3D03038. Could you please look at 3D03039. The date is the 29th. This should make it easier for you to find it. The number again, 3D03039.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier Zarko Tole now sends a notes to UNPROFOR because a truce was signed between the HVO because obviously this offensive lost its momentum, and they realised they had not achieved anything. But you have seen in the book -- in Hodzic's book and Sejtanic's book, that Mr. Izetbegovic says, Well try to take Stolac, because taking Stolac would mean that they could proceed down to Neum. And in spite of this truce that was signed, they go on attacking. And it goes on for days and days, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry. 3D02322. The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The International Red Cross addressed me, asking me to organise -- well, it's the 20th of September. Well, the fighting -- war fighting. I don't know how else to say it. You have seen the number of shells and what it all looked like. To organise again, this lady Carla von Flue, to organise a new round of lectures on international humanitarian law; and since from the IPD in Croatia, they knew that I had done that, this is why she officially addressed me, and I responded, of course, quite promptly. We will see - I don't know - the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D2673. The date is the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, six days later. Of course, I didn't manage to do it sooner because we were still fighting. So six days later, I told her that I agreed fully, that I considered this to be a reasonable request, and I asked her to suggest a time slot for this to actually be done. So this is something that I have to repeat all over again. From the very first time when I started working in the ministry, a primary concern in the Croatian Army and the HVO, to the extent that circumstances actually allowed it, each soldier, each officer, each NCO, was informed about the International Laws of War. Of course, we did not deal with the naval war or neutral countries, but all the basic things when it comes to wartime. Everybody knew that. When I say everybody, I mean 98 percent of the people had to have known that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the number is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I don't know how the Red Cross operates from within, but I'm looking at this official document because it's got a stamp on it. And I note the following: This letter was sent to you, General Praljak, Commander-In-Chief of the HVO, Republic -- Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. So you're given a title. And Herceg-Bosna is, for the Red Cross, a republic. And they are asking you to organise seminars for officers to be trained based on the model of what was done in the Croatian Army in April 1993, so four hours, a group of no more than 30 officers. Very well. It would be interesting, for instance, to know whether the -- not the HVO, whether the Red Cross does the same today with fighters in Iraq, Afghanistan, in Darfur. It would be very interesting to know whether this is a general practice on the part of the Red Cross or whether the Red Cross operates in this way only with organs and institutions the Red Cross recognises as being legal; in which case you were part of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and you were a commander-in-chief. So how is it that you are being sent this mail, this letter, whilst we've heard many witnesses who did not seem to know you? In fact, you didn't seem to be very well known, although here you are known within the Red Cross because we can see your surname. We can't see your first name. We can't see "Slobodan," but we see your surname. So how do you account for the fact that the Red Cross knows you that well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I worked a lot with the International Red Cross while I served in the IPD in the Croatian Army, a lot. We published 100.000 booklets twice. They knew that I was sending those booklets to the HVO, and witnesses testified to that here, that this was being distributed down there too. Secondly, in 1992 and when I was in Central Bosnia, precisely because I was there as somebody who was serving in the Croatian Army, I didn't really tell everyone, shout it from the rooftops that I was there. I tried to do my job as quietly as possible. I would always say, "General," not "General Praljak," while I was doing what I was doing in Mostar. I didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the speaker is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Because it was signed by the international community. Bosniaks and Croats signed that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be set up as a confederation of three republics, and one of them was the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. That was its name. And as far as the Red Cross is concerned, that was an internationally-recognised legal agreement. And the only thing is that I was not the commander-in-chief, that was supposed to be Mate Boban. But probably she thought -- well, she meant to say the commander of the Main Staff, but it's the kind of error that those people in the Red Cross, well, for them the supreme commander of an army, they use those terms interchangeably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How is it, then, that the Red Cross had your fax number, 058-723-729?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, Your Honours, it's not about the Red Cross. I think anyone had the fax number, anyone who wanted to have it, it was available. We never kept anything secret from the journalists or anyone else. Everyone got it. Everybody got passes from the Main Staff to go wherever they pleased to see whatever they pleased. It was just that once there was this BBC reporter who had produced an entirely false report from Konjic. I remained angry with this journalist for about two hours. I said, You won't set foot in Mostar. You go wherever else you like. Two hours later, however, I realised already that my anger made no sense, so I just said, Well, just come on over, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question and then we'll have the break. Isn't there a contradiction between the fact that in the eyes of the Red Cross, you are an army, and they wanted to train your officers; whereas you spent your time telling us that your army was a bunch of untrained soldiers? Isn't there a contradiction here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No contradiction, nor indeed did I term it the way you just phrased it, Your Honour. Any social organisation or structure, such as an army, has all manner and shape of crystallisations within it. The HVO, the part that responded to the call-up, was brave, went out and fought. Many of them were killed. They had within them a sense of justice. So they stood up to things such as smuggling and smugglers, or whenever they saw some municipal officials giving jobs to their relatives instead of soldiers. It was for a sense of justice. Why would I go out to get myself killed? You stay at the back, home and dry. You do whatever you please. I'll take your place in the municipal office, and you go out and get killed. These are different crystallisations. I'm not talking about the HVO like that, but it wasn't structured the way a professional army would have been, with long traditions, 100- 200-year traditions. There was no legal system in place, no judges, no telephones, no offices to go around. But there was this ferment. It wasn't just a crowd. I never said that. I'm not talking about those problems. I'm not talking about the positives. I'm just talking about the number of problems created by certain disruptive groups, which leaves the impression that everyone was like that. But that just isn't true. Those men fought bravely and honorably. They fought the Serbs and fought the BH Army with equal bravery and honour. Nevertheless, certain things happened that were inappropriate and should not have happened under the rules of the International Law of War. But each individual must be made responsible for their own actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have our 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. For the record, when I called the number 3D02763, the number pertains to a document that constitutes a response of General Praljak to 3D02322. We may as well just move on to that document so that we see the whole picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My signature, my response. I fully accept this. We are asking to know what the terms would be -- or, rather, what the date would be, and there is nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all the other microphones be switched off, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my signature, one of my documents. It's about Tihomir Blaskic, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. He obviously submitted some information on how chemical agents were being used. There were no chemical agents being used. Those were irritants being used, not chemical agents. So I'm asking him to provide some accurate information, an organised list, and what exactly was used, what this was about, any medical findings in relation to that, and whether the UN ever established that -- they did establish that irritants were used, but not chemical agents. This was a case of exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 2329 [as interpreted]. The document was produced by Operative Zeljko Akrap. 3D02390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Pinter, but if I look at the record, I see line 20 does not make sense, frankly. I haven't found the document either, because I haven't found the previous one either.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript, line 22, reflects 3D02390.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, and I asked about line 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, what I said was not properly understood. I probably mis-articulated and the number that appeared was erroneous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zeljko Akrap is an operative of the Main Staff, one of those who came from Croatia as a volunteer. Nothing much, really. He says that the HVO forces are tired, exhausted. The most critical situation was over in Ljubuski. The brigade, some of them had abandoned their positions without being replaced. And goes on to discuss the fighting at Zepce, where the Muslim forces had made an effort to take back some positions. There was an attempted infantry attack at Santic Street, and there was fierce fighting in the Podhum area. This was a new attack in an attempt to pierce through defence lines at Mostar. This is a textbook combat report by an operative. He received some information on that day, and he summed this information up in order to produce a collective report and the goings-on along the front-line on that particular day. Nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could I please be helped in finding the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the 24th of September, 1993. The legibility is poor, but I think it should be the 24th of September or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, so that we don't have to get back to this: This operative agent or officer at the Main Staff, who is Mr. Akrap? How long is his tenure? Is it three times eight, is that the kind of shift they have? Or does he come in the morning and leave in the afternoon? Or is there always someone at the Main Staff 24 hours a day, an officer or an operative officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was always an operative officer who was there. The links were always operating at the Main Staff. There were always sufficient officers there to take charge. General Matic, the former JNA officer, his replacement had already retired. He was an elderly gentleman, in relative terms, but then joined the HVO. He was in charge of this. He spent his time drawing maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not answering my question. This operative officer, is he on duty 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the schedule here. I used to work with them, drawing up these schedules. I think there were 12-hour schedules, so they took turns every 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that you, as a commander of the HVO, at 3.00 in the morning, for instance, you could call up this officer who was on duty to give him an order for any kind of order, and this officer on duty, does he hold a log-book in which he writes down, for instance: "10th of September, 1993, call from General Praljak, who is asking me to send him an ambulance"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, there was a book there, a log-book, where document numbers were recorded and everything, a book containing all the structural elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is this log-book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea. I don't think anyone else has, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it destroyed? Did it disappear? Was it stolen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No idea, Your Honours, no information whatsoever that I can provide on that. The book is gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since my questions contain no traps and are not malicious in any way, if that log-book had existed we would have had, for the date of the 9th of May, everything that happened in Sovici and Doljani. This would have been recorded in the log-book. And anything related to Stupni Do would have been recorded in this log-book also; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the documents that arrived and left were recorded, as well as all the relevant elements. Unfortunately, my previous answer is quite accurate. I don't have that. We looked high and low in a bid to find that book, but everything was to no avail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence has the log-book of the Main Staff. This is something that we received from the Prosecutor, but that was the only thing that was made available to us, the documents pertaining to the Main Staff or reaching the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us now move on to P05279, 5279. Your document, General; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date is the 22nd of September, 1993. I specifically state that disciplinary measures, in terms of detention or prison, were being taken, and I, as commander, had the power to impose those, people who were punished, people who saw disciplinary measures taken against them, because the commanders had the power to do that, because these people were the perpetrators and would now serve time in the Dretelj military remand prison -- military remand and prison. That's paragraph 2. Paragraph 3 states that the commanders were required, as were the military disciplinary courts, in addition to the detainee, to attach a disciplinary sentence -- a judgement just to make sure that that person was not there by accident. I tasked all of my commanders to do this properly. I also addressed my own immediate commanders and presidents of the Military Disciplinary Court, in the first instance as well as the second. I asked them to produce the relevant court papers when they bring someone in and any decisions regarding disciplinary measures being taken. Why Dretelj? I had received many complaints from my commanders and soldiers indicating that when disciplinary measures were taken against someone, and that this person had to serve time in Livno, people would make use of their acquaintances, because the warden happened to be his brother, or his cousin, or someone else, and then they would release them to spend an evening in a pub somewhere and then go home. And that violated the authority of the commander, which in turn gave rise to mutiny within the unit itself. This man was punished, yet now he is walking about town free as a bird, having a drink. I then determined that everyone was to remain in Dretelj. At the same time, what this proves to me is that on the 22nd of September, for me, Dretelj was a prison facility that was used for people who had to be there to serve their sentences. Therefore, I am putting it to the Trial Chamber that my knowledge dating back to that time, and the knowledge that we heard here, the information that we heard here, are divergent. On the 22nd of September, 1993, my information on Dretelj indicated that this was a prison, where persons were serving their sentences, HVO soldiers, soldiers, the Muslims, the Croats, officers, soldiers, everyone alike; and everything was done in keeping with the laws and as it had to be done. So that's my understanding of what the document states. If anyone has any questions regarding this, I'd be happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have questions. In light of what you heard about Dretelj, did you -- some victims came to tell us what had happened to them. You are telling us today that this was a military prison. Had you known that civilians were being detained in Dretelj, would you have sent officers or HVO soldiers to go there and be accommodated in the same prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had I known about Dretelj what I heard here at this trial, I would not have done that. My information on Dretelj at the time was the reason that I produced this document the way I did. Had I had other information, I would not have produced this document like this. That is what is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak - I call you General Praljak because that was the position you held - you know that when one is in charge of a command, the notion of control is important. And when a commander sends out an order, he must make sure and check that this order has been carried out. Control and command, therefore, carries its full weight. Why did you not -- I mean, this is an assumption I'm making. Why did you not check on the spot whether HVO soldiers, who had been punished, had been sent to Dretelj? These had been the subject of disciplinary measures. When you went to the prison, you should have seen that there were civilians, and control and command were part of your duties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... for that. First of all, the military investigative prisons were not under the control of the Main Staff at all. These are -- these were separate, independent institution that were run -- well, the Main Staff had nothing to do with them. That's number one. Number two, and this is something I've been saying all along: If you forget, as a symphony, Your Honours, it appears to me that we're just listening to the first violins, then we listen to the second violins a week later, and then the drums and so on, but for -- I am under attack here for two months. This is a war. I have 10 people killed every day. I have many wounded units on the front-line. So the question is when. And even if there were, and there weren't, the question is when. How am I to send out the helicopters for medical evacuations? How can I relieve the troops that had fled their positions? How Petkovic and I and others are to make sure that the wounded are evacuated from Central Bosnia? How am I to violate the embargo and send weapons to Tihomir Blaskic or to Zepce? And it always -- it looks as if we're sitting in a room and looking at the problem in a time-period, how to organise a convoy to evacuate -- all right, yes, I'll speak more slowly. I am claiming that I, and most of my officers that I commanded, worked 20 hours a day. And I controlled, of course, where I had the right to do so, and I punished and controlled -- we punished hundreds of people, and this, A, first of all, was not under my jurisdiction, and I did not have the right to control it. But let's say there is a lull in the fighting and so on, and I received information that I heard here. Had I had this information, then on my own initiative, not as part of the structure that was in place, but as I often acted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
