utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. I believe my colleague also has a question. This is my last question. You have told us that the prisons were not placed under the authority of the Main Staff, so who did the prisons report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will refrain from giving you an answer, because I don't want to interpret what was being said here. No reports from the prisons reached the Main Staff. According to the establishment, we did not have the right to get involved with the prisons. The only duty that I had, the only right that I had, was to send the person, the convict, with the paper stating what they had done, and that's what had to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But Dretelj was a military prison; do you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military investigative or military -- well, it is specified in the documents somewhere, what kind of a prison it was. The fact that it's a military prison does not mean that it was under the Main Staff. The fact that it was called the military prison or military investigative prison, it was an institution that was run by lawyers as part of an organisation. And I don't know, but according to the books that I studied, the Main Staff had nothing to do with the prisons. Furthermore, when I issued the "laissez passer" for the reporter to get in, why shouldn't I do it? He was turned back, and he was told, Praljak had nothing to do with it. And you have a statement by Zeljko Rogosic to that effect. I thought, of course, there was no reason to hide anything there. Let the TV crews get in. The English reporter who testified here on the 8th of September, let Mr. Rogosic from Globus get in. As far as I was concerned, everything was open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we know, in light of the evidence, and I would like to tell you that I don't wish to challenge what you are saying. I'm just stating the facts, and I'll listen to what you are telling us. So we have heard witnesses and evidence that stated the following: The prison is guarded either by home guards, "Domobrani," I believe in your language, either by these people or by military policemen. If the prison is guarded by military policemen, the military policemen are part of the hierarchy. At the head of this hierarchy, there is a commander, the military commander of the HVO, of the military police, and that is you. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, that there is a complete misunderstanding here. We're completely at odds here, and I wonder whether in the three years -- well, the military police has nothing to do with the Main Staff. The military police has its chief, who belongs to a separate department of the Defence Department. It has its tasks, in accordance with its documents, and the Main Staff has no right to issue any orders to the military police. I never received -- I or the Main Staff never received any reports about any prisons. Just a moment. Now, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we would like to try and not waste any time. It's a shame that Mr. Coric is not here, but I'm sure his counsel will inform him. You have told us what your position is. That's fine. But the question I have now is: Do you agree with me that Valentin Coric was at the head of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The chief of an administration in the Defence Department, well, that was, to the best of my knowledge, Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Valentin Coric. As far as you know, was he reporting to whom? Under whose orders was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know who commanded Mr. Valentin Coric, who issued orders to him. Who was the superior of the chief? Well, I'm sure that the chief of the military police could not be under the command of the commander of the Main Staff. He commanded, in operational a terms, the units of the military police when they were resubordinated to him during some combat operations for a limited period of time. But functionally, they remained part of their own structure. The same went for the military. Medical service, IPD was an independent service, the SIS; so they were all parallel systems within what is termed the military component of the HVO, aside from the political one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Praljak, I have had this question at the back of my mind for some time, but you've answered part of my question. Nonetheless, I would still like to put my question to you. I have understood that the military prisons did not come under the authority of the Main Staff. That I understood. I also understood that you did not receive any reports from the military police. So my question is a very straightforward one. What happens when your soldiers, who were detained in Dretelj, had problems, whatever these problems may have been, people who were taken ill, people who died, people who filed complaints because they were unhappy with the food or the medicine they had been given? In that case, did the Main Staff that you belonged to not take any notice of these men? Were you still in contact? Did you still know what was happening in the prison or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, this is a hypothetical question. Had I received some reports from some lad who complained about the structure or through a structure about improper conduct or treatment in prison, I would definitely have done something for him. I would have stood up for him. But I never received any reports from any prisons about any improper treatment of soldiers, officers, or NCOs of the HVO serving their disciplinary sentence, disciplinary sentence. Disciplinary -- these are disciplinary measures that we had the right to impose. Now, as for criminal offences, we, the Main Staff of the HVO, did not have any jurisdiction there, any powers. This was a separate legal system. For disciplinary measures, you simply take a piece of paper and you punish such and such a person. You sentence him to two weeks in prison, and there is no trial, no defence case. This is the discretionary right of the commander. And I had the right to impose higher sentences than brigade commanders. Well, it's all stipulated which commander has the right to impose what sentence. But if a crime is committed, then you have the court, the prosecution, the trial, the cases of the two parties, and the Main Staff has nothing to do with it anymore. And now as for the serving of those sentences, I did not have any complaints, not a single document, not a single oral or written complaint, about any improper treatment of any of my soldiers during the service of their sentences ever. Nothing of the sort ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small intervention regarding the transcript. At page 50, line 7, the translation misses a word that General Praljak said, and I was following quite carefully, and it's the word "parallel." General Praljak said that Medical Service, IPD and SIS, and he also mentioned the military police, are parallel components, together with the military component of the HVO. The word "parallel "is not in the transcript, and it's very important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, these are parallel components that have their own chiefs, their duties, their rights, their powers, and they are performing them, and they do some things as part of those things. So if you have a doctor in a military unit, he's part of the healthcare service. But when the unit goes out in the field, he goes together with them. And then when an operation is planned, he says, Well, I need such and such things. And he asks how many casualties are anticipated, prepares the cars, and arrangements are made for the evacuation of the first echelon and the second echelon. So he's doing his job within his structure. This assists the commander of a brigade or of a zone to plan the operation as it should be done. And this is how it's done in other armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, when my Brother Mindua asked you how you would have reacted if there had been a complaint, you, without hesitating, said, I would have ordered an investigation. On what authority would you have done that? I thought, and before you told us, that you had no authority whatsoever. Now say you would order an investigation. On what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the basis of somebody mistreating my man, and then I had the power to ask why this person was mistreated. I would ask who was there. I would ask for an explanation. The right to control and to ask -- the right to ask what happened to my soldier, these are two separate things, Judge Trechsel. After all, Amnesty International does not have any powers over prisons and human rights violations, and yet they demand that reports be issued and that they be told what is going on. So these are two different sets of rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I do not find this at all convincing. I mean, if you can order an investigation, you could well go and preventively look whether things are all right. That's what I must conclude. I find your contrary assertions not convincing. And another point -- this was more a statement than a question, actually. But of course you can react to it. I seem to recall that earlier on in this trial, in quite a different context, you have rather proudly declared how open you were and that you had given a television team of ZDF, the second German television chain, a permission to visit -- I think, it was Gabela and not Dretelj, but a prison. Do I remember wrongly or how did you have that authority at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I think that for I don't know what reason add to my words, the words that I never said. I didn't say that I would have demanded or ordered an investigation. That's not what I said, and it's really strange that you add to what I have said and that you cannot create systems that divine from my words. To demand that an investigation be carried out is not to order that an investigation be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it may be that what you said was not properly interpreted because I heard the French booth and it said that you could have ordered an investigation. Hence the question put by my fellow Judge. What did you say exactly in your own language. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these are very precise things, and you have to understand them in that way. If I learned -- whenever I learned that something was going on that was not in line with the rules, the regulations, or the law, I first, A, ordered that an investigation be carried out within my powers, within my purview or jurisdiction; B, I demanded that an investigation be carried out in those areas over which I had no jurisdiction. And when I - we saw the document - demanded that those police be arrested, I did not write an order for those police to be arrested and to be put in prison. And we saw that yesterday, but I demanded, because I had learned. Valentin Coric had not learn that. He did not have this information. I had this information. And I forwarded this information to Mate Boban, to Mr. Valentin Coric, and I say here, these people, according to the information that I have, and I'm claiming that this is correct, did this or that. And I demand, not "I order," I demand that you put them in prison. That's one thing. And, secondly, when Ms. Ivanisevic contacted me, asking me that they would like to get "laissez passer." It is true -- or Vujami [phoen], whatever his name is, the British reporter, Vujami. He says, yeah, I asked that from Mate Boban's office and I didn't get it. And then I met General Praljak, and he, to my surprise - that's what he said, and I asked him why to his surprise - wrote that to me. There are two possibilities here: That I am saying what Judge Trechsel is saying. This is not under my jurisdiction. I don't care if you are going there to film or not. The fact that this is not under my jurisdiction, that I did not have any power over it, did not prevent me from writing a "laissez passer," and, then if it works, well it's going to work, and if not, it's not going to work. So I took this position: Nothing is to be concealed. In accordance with the strictest of rules, I was not supposed to write it. And they were not supposed to get in anywhere with "laissez passer." And this is what happened to the other journalists. But when I wrote that, I didn't do it -- and this -- so as to indicate that I had a right to do it. So what I said, Judge Trechsel, is correct. I couldn't order. I could only demand, and these are two different terms. And I always, be it within the framework of what I could do as a commander under the law, reacted if I considered that there were any violations. But this doesn't mean that I had the right to do it or that it was my duty to do it. It was my obligation as a human being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I just want to recall, Mr. Praljak, I'm a bit surprised at this formalism which you present now, after having told us many times that you didn't care very much about regulations; for instance that you went and you said what had to be done, when you were not appointed in any official way, and everybody obeyed you. So to tell us now, the Chamber, that you could have not looked at your soldiers in a prison if you had wanted to, for formal reasons, I simply have to tell you it is not entirely convincing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, I didn't say that. I didn't say what you just said. I am sorry, but please tell me where exactly I said that I could not send my soldiers into prison. Can you please quote me exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There must be -- either I misspoke or a problem in translation. I was speaking about your possibility to go into a prison, where soldiers which were under your command, by yourself, one of your sub-commanders had been sent into the prison, that you could not have gone and see whether they are dealt with in a correct way. I never challenged your right to send people. That was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, please, I never said that either. I never said that I could not access the prison. I could access the prison. And it is highly likely that no one would have been able to stop me. All I'm saying is the following: I did not have any reason to go there because I never received any reports or information that would have prompted me to go there. Why on earth would I go there if I previously had seen no information that there was anything untoward going on, to my soldiers or to anyone else? That's one thing. The other thing is I had a war going on at my door-step, Judge Trechsel, a war. I have no idea what we spent the last three years talking about. What about the 7.000 dead, HVO soldiers who were killed, young lads? What about the 10.000 wounded who were there? What about all the shells that were fired? What about all the wounded, 15.000 or whatever? I have no idea. I'll tell you one thing, if I may. For example, my refugees, the Muslims, in my holiday cottage -- I spent some time there that winter, and then I got in touch with a friend who was wounded. He was a war invalid from the HVO. That winter, I bought a calf in Slavonia, and I sent half that calf back home and the other half I left there. But if, at the moment of the attack on Hum everything else altogether, when I had 10 people who had been killed, and 15 or 20 wounded, then if you told me at that point in time that poor food was being served to someone in prison, at that point in time there would have been no reaction on my part to poor food being served. God forbid, for example, you have children and your child takes seriously ill, or someone else's child, and then someone tells you, Well, you know what, you have a leak in your bathroom. This is only a minor manner. At the time, obviously, if I had heard about worse things, I would have reacted. But there's a thread of tolerance to anything that goes on even in a war. If I need helicopters to evacuate the wounded, about 50 of those per day, even if I found out, for example, that poor food was being served in that prison, well, poor food, what can I say? I can hardly remember what I was eating myself. It certainly wasn't proper food. What we're talking about here is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we understand what you say very well. You are saying that there were 7.000 soldiers HVO soldiers killed and 10.000 wounded. Very well, nobody challenges that, and not the judges in the first place. But that's not the problem. The problem is that this Tribunal has to try a case in which international humanitarian law is involved, and you, as I, listened to the victims who testified here at the very spot where you're sitting today. And like me, you heard some speak about the conditions in which they were detained, so you know that. The Judges will have to determine whether and to what extent you may be liable for what happened. That's the basic problem. Furthermore, you told us, and you showed us evidence, that you authorised a journalist to go and visit a prison. Nobody challenges that. But we have to see this authorisation that you gave within its proper context. And when I learned this, and this is quite a few months back, straight away I thought this, and I'll tell you what I then thought straight away. If there was a joint criminal enterprise through which civilians are being detained, mistreated, some of them killed, is a journalist going to be authorised to enter a prison facility to see what is there to be seen and draw conclusions that are going to be made public to the entire world? That was my question back then, because everybody knows the weight of the media. You can easily imagine that if a journalist had been to this notorious prison in Iraq, he or she would have immediately reported on what may have happened there. So when I saw this document, saying that you gave the permission, I immediately made a connection with a possible joint criminal enterprise. I was planning to ask you, the question, but this is very topical now. So I may as well put my question now. You are under oath, so this will make the approach easier. When this journalist came to ask you this permission to go to this prison, did you, yourself, call other authorities, Mate Boban, Stojic, or Prlic, to tell them, Look, there's a problem. There's an international reporter who wants to come and have a look at what's happening in prison; that may cause problems. What am I to do? Did you call them or did you say, Well, I have a human responsibility. Someone tells me they want to visit a prison. I've got nothing to hide, and I gave them leave even if this is not within my purview, because as a human being I have nothing to hide? Now, what was your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This last inference of yours, I called no one. Within eight days, I let in three journalists, the ZDF, the German crew, was the first; not really let them in, I granted them permission to go, and that's just it. I had nothing to conceal. I believe, and it is my position, that nothing must be concealed. I expect the honourable Chamber to reach that correct inference eventually, in terms of determining my responsibility regarding that. Should the Chamber, along with the OTP, find any proof, any evidence, any information that I had at the time about what was going on over there in any of the reports, you will hand down a sentence and you will say, Praljak, you are to remain in prison for a number of years. What I'm telling you is I had no information on those detention centres or prisons indicating that there was anything untoward happening there. In this text, the piece by the Globus journalist, I read that some reclining chairs or beds were missing there. And then I called the Capljina barracks and I said, If you have a surplus, please take the settees or reclining chairs over there so they can use them. That is all I knew at the time, and that is why I wrote this text on the 22nd. Based on today's information, the information that I'm aware of today - if what we have heard here is true, I would not go into that - I would not have dispatched my own lads there, the brigade soldiers, to go to prison there. I would not have done that. They were not under my jurisdiction. I received no reports from anyone on the situation there, none at all. And at the time, I knew nothing about that, not on any basis whatsoever. If you have a document or the OTP has documents proving that what I'm saying is a lie, you'll write up a sentence for me. There you go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I asked you the question, and your answer has been recorded. Anybody can refer to it, and no doubt the Prosecutor will revisit the issue when they cross-examine you. But I might, too, because there are many topics to address, and we don't have all the time in the world. So your conclusion, as you say, is that, I was not in the know of anything, I was not aware of anything. That is your conclusion. Very well. We'll keep it in mind. Please proceed, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can you please go to 3D02057 [Realtime transcript read in error "3D020257"].

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that document. It's a document signed by the chief of SIS in Rama, Luka Markesic, on the 23rd of September. He is taking stock of the war in Rama by the 20th of September, 1993. There is nothing to add: The number of women and children killed; the number of civilian casualties; the number of soldiers wounded in a brigade that was a small brigade, not a large one, 188; the number of soldiers killed, 61; and so on and so forth. This is an accurate report, very specific, on what was really going on on the ground. And this is something that I was unfortunately involved in, unfortunately or fortunately, depending on how you decide to approach this. Fortunately, we did not end up being the losers. They did not manage to beat us. Unfortunately, because that kind of involvement leads you to a fate like this. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It seems that I will have to go and see a specialist about this, because I can't seem to get a single number right. Can we please have the tape listened to? This is 3D02057, the document number. Please state the date also, because that is another error.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Next up is P05350.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my document, the 24th of September, 1993. It's a textbook military order at the time when the BH Army were infiltrating the saboteurs behind our lines. I believe some of our men were killed. I think we discussed this at one point, but there's nothing to add, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about the introduction to this document, two orders that you wrote? Can you please comment on those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No comment. The order is clear. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Please go to 3D01171.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one of my orders. The date is -- I can't say, but about the 25th of September, 1993. Yes, the 25th of September, 1993. There is a misunderstanding between the commanders, and one still has to teach them that it is their duty to communicate, to think, to do everything. But at one point in time, it is down to the commander to take a decision. And the decision must then be carried out, and then no further adieu about that, no discussion. A commander has every right to change his decision. Today he makes one decision, the next day he makes a different decision. He's perfectly within his rights because the situation changes on a daily basis as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: P05402. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. A question on the previous document. Did we see the order that is rendered invalid here?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean 3D01171, that question, the order from the Main Staff being rendered invalid, paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what is being rendered invalid here. I can't be expected to remember what exactly it was I was rendering invalid at the time. But why -- there must have been some sort of misunderstanding, quite obviously. The commander and his deputy commander probably provided two different bits of information. They couldn't reach an understanding, and the order of the Main Staff was probably erroneous. But I don't think that bears any relevance in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevertheless, we can look for it, if there is a document like that, and then we can show it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I request from Croatia General Brigadier Imra Agotic, who was the head of Croatia's air force, to make it possible for me to have four pilots trained and four MI-8 helicopter technicians in the Divulje base near Split. This would take about 15 days, starting the 28th of September. I assert that this was very difficult to achieve. Mr. Agotic always had some follow-up questions to ask, and I assert it was far easier to get pilots trained by the BH Army than it was for me to get training for my HVO pilots from the Croatian Army. I hereby assert that. There were always follow-up questions: Did we receive approval from the BH Army; did we this; did we that, leading me at one point in time, when he was stopping some of my helicopters from taking off, to act in a brutal manner and use a lot of foul language because we were looking at some wounded from Central Bosnia. Back in his office, he simply failed to understand what the situation was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fair enough. Next up is --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. More proof yet that we are here addressing a different country, as simple as that. There is no communality there. One country, the Banovina, the Croats. It's like -- it's like I'm addressing the Swiss Army or the French Army, asking them to train my pilots additionally and charge a fee for that. The same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: May we have your comments on document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing escapes my notice, General Praljak, and something has just caught my eye. You are asking here for pilots to -- helicopter pilots to be trained. Very well. So you send a letter, and I see that in this letter you refer to order 560-01/09 from the 10th of August, from the Republic of Croatia. So you're quoting a document from the Republic of Croatia, whilst we know that you are on the ground. You are everywhere, but for the prisons, but that you told us already; still you signed a document referring to a document coming from the Republic of Croatia. How is it that you could be informed of the document coming from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because that document is one that the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia wrote on the basis of my request, pursuant to my request, to grant permission for the training of these pilots, six pilots, or additional training, I mean, additional training. And General Agotic did not implement that. That's one point. Let me make it clearer, Judge Antonetti, if I may. For flights to Central Bosnia, when the BH Army blocked all the roads running into Central Bosnia, we had pilots from Russia, excellent pilots, and we paid them. However, that too was organised by Mr. Stojic and, in part, me. Now, since they were attacked several times and targeted several times, these people just lost it - as we say without too much psychology - and didn't want to fly anymore, regardless of the fact that we offered them double the pay and triple the pay. They said they wouldn't be flying anymore because they were afraid to. And now the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were in the Yugoslav People's Army previously, mostly flew planes, and there were five or six of them, and one of them went with this Russian towards Central Bosnia. They flew to Central Bosnia because they were born there. And so they learnt how to fly the helicopter by sitting next to this Russian as co-pilots. And as there was the danger that Central Bosnia or, rather, Blaskic would fall completely, I asked them -- I begged them on my knees -- I begged them to fly. The pilot said he didn't know how to fly the helicopter well enough yet, and so on. The situation was very critical. And as we're talking about what is sometimes erroneously interpreted by His Honour Judge Trechsel, at one point in time, begging your pardon, I took my pants off and said, Well, I'll give you, you know, those things of mine if you do. So after that, that flew hundreds of sorties, saved lots of people, and you can read this in the statements that are attached to the documents of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, when you answer a question, whatever the question may be, I try to put it in one or another category, Defence or Prosecution evidence. You told us that when you asked Agotic to train some of the pilots, some of the men sometimes said, Do you have the agreement of the BiH? You said this very quickly, and then you moved on to something else. So I said to myself that I needed to think about this before I put the question to you because it's an important question. And now I've reached a stage where I can phrase my question. When somebody provides an answer like this, does this mean that in the minds of the people before you, they were providing you with equipment under the condition that this was part of the struggle against the Serbs, but that this was also in agreement with the ABiH. And that is why they then checked to see whether the ABiH agreed to providing you with trainers to train the pilots? As far as you remember, the agreement with the ABiH, was this something that was sufficiently airtight, was it something which you needed, and was that agreement enough, and how involved was the ABiH when it came to providing authorisations to send in additional supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No agreement with the BH Army at all. There was none, nor should there have been, nor did we need to ask permission from the BH Army. Why? Because the BH Army didn't ask me for permission. We were on a footing of equality. They were flying their helicopters. These were HVO helicopters. These were HVO pilots. These people were born on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were volunteers of the HVO, these pilots here. And then, next, on the 10th of August, I asked the minister to enable these pilots to be additionally trained, and then he issued -- well, Mr. Imra Agotic, on the 20th of September -- I repeat this, in fact. So who is Imra Agotic, that I discuss this with him? He -- from the representative of the civilian authorities, and the minister of defence of the civil authority in the Republic of Croatia, to train my men, using my helicopters for my money, as he was doing for the BH Army in Split, Rijeka and Zagreb without any money? He was a general, and he has to listen to the orders he's given. Now, for some reason of his own, best known to him, he tried to side-step this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The general is speaking much too fast, and on page 66, line 17, what the general said has not been recorded, and that is that in Split and Rijeka, pilots of the helicopters belonging to the BH Army were being trained free of charge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In Split, Rijeka and Zagreb, they had their logistic centres, and the pilots were trained there. The helicopters were transport -- flown across Croatia, and this was made possible for the BH Army, whereas this man here was dangling me on a string for a month and a half until I put my foot down and shouted at him and told Gojko Susak to get him off my back. And he got him off my back. So for money, this training was completed. So why would I ask the BH Army for permission, then, when it was doing the same thing in Croatia? Better than vis-a-vis the HVO because they were hot-heads of this type who, like many others, thought that the BH Army was the only army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, General Praljak. Sometimes you go off on a tangent, and I try to ask you to get back to the point. You've told us already, but it's good that you reminded us of this. You told us that the Republic of Croatia was training pilots of the ABiH in Split and Rijeka. If I understand correctly, in September 1993, the ABiH had trained pilots in Split and in Rijeka; is that right? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They had sent their pilots earlier on, Your Honour, and we saw documents to that effect. They had their logistic centres at this point in time. Yes, I will speak slowly. Let me take it slowly. The BH Army at this particular time had -- the Main Staff of the BH Army had its logistic centres that Split, Samobor, Zagreb. As you saw from the documents, they were amassing weapons, purchasing weapons, and we would allow them to pass through our territory at this particular time. And we were doing this clandestinely, secretly from our own people. But under 15 oaths here, I say that even at this time we let through convoys of weapons, not humanitarian aid but convoys carrying weapons and fuel and ammunition for the BH. And you have evidence of that in reports by a very important man connected with armament on their side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ABiH was trained by the Republic of Croatia. I assume that from the logistical bases of the ABiH, the aircraft of the ABiH had to be overhauled. This was done by the Republic of Croatia or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means I can establish a connection with the criminal enterprise. If there's a criminal enterprise in which Tudjman, Susak, Boban, and you are included, does this mean that the criminal enterprise that aims at annexing part of Herzegovina, of ethnically cleansing some of the people, would it be logical then to be in charge of maintaining or overhauling the equipment of those people one wishes to crush so that the Croats in Herzegovina are in the majority? From your perspective, is this logical or illogical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an extremely illogical assumption. It is -- it cries out for want of understanding, because the Croats are 90 percent in the majority in Herzegovina, more than 90 percent. So there can't be more of them than there already are. And I claim, Judge Trechsel and Your Honours, that had this kind of situation faced the French, if something like this was happening to the French, 50 million Frenchmen would have laughed out loud at an indictment of this kind, that you're arming them, that you're supplying them with fuel, that you're seeing to the wounded and sick, and that that then is a joint criminal enterprise. That is something that my head just can't take. There's never been the like in history. But there you have it. We're a small people, a small nation, so you can perform these illogical mental acrobatics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, Judge Antonetti asked you about the operations duty, so look at 3D01161, which is the next document, please. And you mentioned your order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my order and shows what the situation was like. Of course, after all these years, with the passage of time, I, myself, can't quite remember everything and things like this. Anyway, the document speaks for itself. It speaks about combat readiness. It says what the duty mean -- what duty shift means. It analyses the duty operations officers. And the shifts that last for seven days, they are replaced every 12 hours or whatever. And then there is a list of who takes up their duties when. The first group, Petkovic, Keza; and the second you have Tole; third, Stanko Matic, and so on and so forth, officers, non-commissioned officers and whatever. It's all there, all described and set out there. It speaks for itself, and I have no further comments to make.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the next document is P05580.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, this is my order, but I didn't sign it, but that doesn't matter. General Petkovic signed for me, and it's an order -- well, it says that winter is coming and that the war and the fighting won't be over soon. Your Honours, we were fully conscious of the fact that the BH Army certainly had intentions to and would try to -- well, whatever truce or cease-fire was signed, there would be changes in the Vance-Owen and Stoltenberg plans, and all these plans that were signed and whatever. But there was no firm stand taken on the part of the international community to have what it proposed be carried out. If they thought it was wise and logical and sustainable and so on, that it be put into practice, and then that they say that's how it's going to be from now on, as is the case with some other states, the Taliban and whatever. They say -- they put their foot down and say, This is how it's going to be. But, unfortunately, we had a different fate. Anyway, all this is set out in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D02788 is the next document, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 3rd of October, signed by General Petkovic for me, because it says "for," "za."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That means that you agreed with the document and that it was, in fact, your document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it is noted here that the brigade from Posusje did not take over its area of responsibility. And the question was why, why the order was not acted on. And a request is made to investigate and to deal with the matter. So all these documents testify to the problems that arose and how they were solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, these orders show that there is a problem. The commander of the 5th Brigade of Posusje - I apologise for my pronunciation - was he someone who could be contacted over the telephone? Couldn't you call him up and tell him, How is it that you haven't been deployed, rather than issuing orders on paper? Wouldn't it have been possible to ask him to give you an explanation over the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very frequently, no, Your Honour. No, we couldn't do it by telephone very often. And it's always a good idea to leave a written trace, so this was as fast as a telephone communication. He needn't have been in the command. He might have been somewhere in the field, but this document would arrive and he would have had to have received it. So the telephone is a relatively unreliable means of communication because soldiers don't sit in their offices. They have other things to attend to. But, anyway, the duty officer's there to receive the order, and then he hands it over to the commander once the commander arrives because the commander's probably somewhere with his brigade, manning a position of some sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, do you know, but maybe this is something that you don't know, that one of the military principles or tenets is that in the chain of command, between the bottom and the top, there needs to be a permanent contact so that the orders can be disseminated and that the leaders can be informed; and if there is no such contact or the contact is lost, this can give rise to problems? I'm sure this applied to the JNA. Was this not applied in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, principles are one thing, and at least in Croatian the verb and the conditional "must" and "should" and so on doesn't mean a lot. What means a lot is what you can do and what you have at your disposal, and all your principles fall through if you cannot realise something because you don't have the means to realise it with. Now, as for communications, and I could go on talking about communications for days, the 1st Division, the 1st famous Marine Division, which numbered 21.000 soldiers, roughly, has 28.000 communication lines amongst themselves, simultaneous ones. Now, a thousandth of that we did not have. We had the packet link -- packet communication that was down sometimes. We had very poor telephone communications, which functioned towards Split but were very often down towards other places. So as for communication, especially if somebody is out in the field, to get in contact with a company or whatever out in the field at their positions, the kind of devices you need to have, and then have coded communication, well, certainly not. We didn't have any of that. Principles are principles. Principles are one thing, but whatever the principles are, you either have the devices or you don't. You have the money for them or you don't. And even if you have the money, they're not readily available. You can't just go out and purchase some good military equipment whenever you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at document P05702. Again, is that yours down there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not my signature. Somebody signed it in my stead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But do you agree with the contents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, with the contents of the document. Again, I address Gojko Susak, and I probably told him orally, Please send this. But this is not my signature, and I'm asking for two cannons to be replaced because of wear and tear. I want him to give me two cannons that are in good working order, and I actually want to get him to rent me a Howitzer battery. And this is what I'm asking for, and I didn't get it. I got some, and I didn't get other things. And I repeat, the money for this purchase, as we heard testimony, was the money from Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina that transferred the money to a joint account for the defence of Croats against the aggression. So I had the right to ask that for the money given by the people who gave the money who fought down there to be given this. I got some of it, but I didn't get the Howitzer battery. I think we managed to replace the barrels. But, again, this speaks -- yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Could the general please clarify the date of the document? I'm looking at the date in the top part, and both the original and the translation has too many numbers. I wonder if you could clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's not too many numbers. The date from Citluk is the 7th of October. Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, 24, it's too much.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 24, somebody probably just put it there. But as I was not going there, and I was contacted at the forward command post at Prozor, well, that's where the forward command post was. And it is fairly certain that on the 12th of October I said, Send this, regardless of the fact that I was not there, and sign it, because I agree with the request.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So the date is the 7th of October?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. General Praljak, as far as the date is concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, it's obvious that this text is written on the 7th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this request was a request which was coded or was it transmitted to Mr. Susak via packet switching system? I'm asking you this question against the backdrop of what is going to follow. Generally speaking, when I put a question to you, there is -- it's never a trick question. You know that at the time at the UN Security Council, the intervention of the Croatian Army in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was being discussed. Let's imagine that at the time your request was something which was known. In that case, we would have said, There is proof of the fact that the Republic of Croatia is helping the HV. So when you send this kind of letter to Mr. Susak, this is being sent in a coded fashion or don't you feel that this is a problem at all because you've got nothing to hide? You are asking to have two 130-millimetre barrels and so on, so as far as you're concerned this is a perfectly standard request filed by the union of the republics - this is what's indicated in the title of the document - of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Was this 100 percent confidential because on the document it says "Classified?" Well, military secret and generally speaking, when the military sends something, it's always classified or a military secret. Did you not consider that when this was being sent out, if this had been made known, this was a proof that the Army of the Republic of Croatia was helping the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No protection, no concern. This was sent only by fax, probably. Of course, whoever wants to -- any well-trained organisation can get at those faxes. We are in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I request that the following demands be met, and that's the replacement of two T-130-millimetre cannon because of wear and tear. And further on, if the Croats from Croatia can send this with our cooperation to the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina, if we can send fuel so their helicopters can fly, making 500 sorties, as they say themselves -- one helicopter did 500 sorties, so I don't see why they should not assist in parallel two armed forces which are in conflict at this present point in time. And I would like to show that to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We need to have a break very soon. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you now please look at 3D00 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we could not hear the number because of the noise in our microphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date is the 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, there was a noise in our microphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D00779. The document is dated the 8th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's your document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my document, my signature. And at that time, the cease-fire was already signed. And I learned that at one point there was an aeroplane that was flying around without my approval. And I say that they shall not fly without my approval or without the approval of a person that I shall authorise, except when they are evacuating the wounded. And on those occasions because urgency is important, and they might not be able to get in contact with me, and this has to do with what Judge Antonetti asked me about the communications, then they can fly. They can make that decision themselves, and then it will be approved ex-post-facto. And there is an order also to the effect that the artillery should not fire any rounds without the approval from somebody from the Main Staff, and this is lest somebody should fire at will and violate the cease-fire; although you should not place the artillery under the command because it is under the command of the operational zones. This is not in accordance with military logic. But at that time, this seemed to be sound to me, and they always had to inform the Main Staff if they wanted to target something and explain why they wanted to target it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. Praljak, that you are speaking about an order which is not this one. This one does not refer to artillery, so it's not very helpful because it's in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do apologise. I did stray a bit, and I do apologise, Your Honour. I wanted to establish some sort of a connection, but I will not do that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a quarter to 6.00. We need to have our 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please look at document 3D02766. It's a document of the 9th of October, 1993, and you are the signatory?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document, and I am asking -- well, this shows the difference between an order and a demand or a request. So from the Military Police Administration in Ljubuski, I'm asking something. And I'm sending this to the operational zone in Tomislavgrad. I'm asking them to put at the disposal a military police unit in order to bring in the conscripts from Jajce who are in the Livno municipality. And there are 191 such conscripts. And these people should simply be brought in and put into their units, because they are military conscripts, subject to military obligation, and they are violating the law on mobilisation, the law on draft. That's as much as I can say about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I try to see whether there is any contradiction in what you say. Sometimes I do notice there are some contradictions, and I tell you straight away whenever that is the case, to clear all this up. So in the afternoon, you explained what the HVO Army was, and I thought I had understood that it was made up of volunteers, and that in the end you had little authority over them, and now we find a document that says the opposite. Indeed, and you said so yourself a minute ago, these are conscripts, so they could not elude their military obligations. And if they tried to, they have to be arrested by the military police. So there is an apparent contradiction between what you said this afternoon and this document. How can you settle this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, there is no contradiction. If those people left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Herceg-Bosna and went to Croatia -- or, rather, this is what I'm talking about. They could have gone, and that's why those who remained there are in some way volunteers. This is a unit from Jajce. So when Jajce fell, of course they scattered around, and some of them went back and so on, but there are 191 of them. And I am demanding from the military police to bring them in, since they are there. So the first division is the division between those who could leave across the border and those who couldn't. Had these people left and crossed the border, and this is why those who are left are volunteers, even if they are brought in. Why? Because they couldn't find accommodation or because their families were there. I'm not going to go into that. So a military was not a volunteer force. There was a draft, and they had to respond to the call-up. And if they failed to do that, the military police brought them in. And there were, well, so many reports, that they couldn't be found, that they're not at their proper address, and so on and so forth, but when they were in the territory. But all those who didn't want to take part simply went to Germany, Croatia, France, wherever, to stay with their friends, relatives. And a huge number of people from the HZ-HB, Croats, had been working abroad for 10 or 15 years all over Europe as workers temporarily employed abroad, and everybody could find somebody to stay with. So let me repeat, there is no contradiction, because if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a nutshell, and you say whether it is right or not, those who would remain in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they had to be mobilised because there were conscripts; however, those that had gone abroad, when they would return, they returned as volunteers; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the first part is correct. Those who stayed there, who went on living there, were subject to the military obligation, to the conscription. But how could you explain that in any different way, Your Honour? If you cannot punish somebody who has left, you are left with the volunteers, regardless of whether they are trying to dodge the draft or not. I think that the situation is clear, because if somebody remained there and some responded to the call-up, and others for some reason had to be brought in because they didn't want to go at that particular time because they had some other stuff to do, there were hundreds of reasons why some of them did not want to respond to the call-up specifically to go out into the field on that day. But let me repeat, nobody was punished for dodging the draft, those who had left. There was no law in place. You couldn't say, And now you're going to serve time in prison because you betrayed your country, in effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, did the HVO have barracks, and were all the soldiers in barracks?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, it just had a barracks in Capljina, one in Central Bosnia. I don't know. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, where were the soldiers, then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At home. We've said that a hundred times. As soon as they went back from their positions, they would go home. They would be civilians. They would do some work. So if they received a salary, say, of 120 German marks, they had women, children, they had to live off something. So that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Now would you take a look at the next document, which is 3D00975, and the date is the 12th of October, 1993. It is the Rama Brigade, the Deputy Commander Petar Kolakusic. What can you tell us about that document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by Petar Kolakusic. But it was compiled based on my explicit request for this type of meeting to be held, and the reason is set out here; because inter-human relations had been upset, there were incidents breaking out in town, and the situation was out of control using the normal means and resources open to the civilian authorities or military authorities or whatever. It was out of control. And then I requested that this meeting be convened, and here we have who attended; Guardian, et cetera, the chief, the commander of the military police, the commander of the operations zone, the president of the HVO, Mr. Jozic, who was in jeopardy over there because people kept threatening him. And I'll address that in due course. Well, I can tell you now. Anyway, this is a very good document for that. Your Honours, those who fled abroad from Rama, for example, then the people who stayed on would set fire to their houses, and this happened to four or five houses, Croats setting fire to Croatian houses. That is to say, a fighter, a combatant, would utter some expletives and swear and say he's fled abroad. And they were powerless to do anything else, but they did set their houses on fire. And then they would threaten, asking for money, threaten him with a pistol, ask for money; Mr. Jozic, that is. And then when Mr. Jozic was threatened by this one person who demanded 30.000 marks on the spot or he'd kill him, he called me up, and I sent the command of the military police because the civilian police force wasn't functioning properly. I sent him out to take that man into custody, whereas he asked me for 30.000 marks with a pistol pointed at me, and that's how things were. Now, I managed -- well, the man was quite mad and drunk, and I managed to appease him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. The sentence on lines 14, 15, up to 16, is not clear. It reads: "I sent him out," and him, that's the command of the military police, or the commander, "to take that man into custody, whereas he asked me for 30.000 marks with a pistol pointed at me, and that's how things were." Who asked 30.000 marks from you; the police commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I was speaking much too fast. When the command of the military police went over there, then that man told -- put a pistol to the police chief's head and brought him to my office in Rama-Prozor. And then he threatened me as well and said that he was to be brought 30.000 Deutschmarks on the spot, or he'd kill us all, he'll kill me. Now, a little while after that, the president of the municipality, this man Jozic, Mr. Jozic, once again -- well, he just lost it. He couldn't take the situation anymore. And he got into his car, switched the engine on, and drove off to Germany and never returned. Now, I understand the man. But some people, despite all those terrible problems, had to remain. And the person who had to remain seems to be to blame now for having stayed. So you have witness statements about that event. And just like the events in Travnik, I filmed all this, and I'll show what it looks like when some idiot is threatening to shoot you with a pistol unless you give him 30.000 marks on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, what were the circumstances under which this meeting was held? Did you have any private --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this meeting and another meeting, when I managed to gather a much broader circle of people together, I stayed on despite the fact that I was told that my father had died. And I had to go to Zagreb and see to the paperwork so that his bodily remains be brought to Herzegovina. But despite that, I stayed on. I didn't go to Zagreb. I postponed going. I asked them to wait for me because the problems in Rama had exceeded what was acceptable. They'd gone beyond what was acceptable. People were doing all sorts of things during the day and during the night. So I composed this group of people. Then I added more people. I did that, and then you can't issue orders. You can talk to the people and treat them, explain them, request things of them, ask them to do something, ask them to be more involved, from the priests, everyone, to take part and to help out, things that have nothing to do with the conduct of the army and military establishment. That's the truth of it. Now, how you're going to understand this and interpret it, I really don't know. I'm telling you how the facts were, the bare facts, naked facts, in human terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the next document, which is 3D02397.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document. I know Mr. Brekalo. That is one of the people who went -- who came down there as a volunteer. He was also a fighter in Vukovar because he hails from that general area. And he helped out in a lot of aspects, in a military and friendly way, and here's what he says. Well, I sent him to tour the front-line, and he's reporting back to me and telling me what he found there. So there's nothing that I can add there. The document speaks for itself; who were the fatalities and casualties, how many people, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what about the MTS, materiel and technical equipment situation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he says that 82-millimetre mortars, that there were two of those, that they hadn't been cleaned properly, that the cannon hadn't -- canyon hadn't been mined properly, and that the obstruction hadn't been properly carried out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now we come to 3D02148, dated the 21st of October, 1993, and you signed that document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign this document. It's one of my documents. Once again, it says that the military conscripts from Kakanj and Vares have arrived with a convoy of refugees, and that's it. It asks that the conscripts should report and then be deployed to the brigades. And I say who should be in charge of all this and how this should be done, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's go on to 3D02795, which is also one of your documents.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature there. So these people from the Lasva Battalion, who were in Capljina, at the barracks there, I asked that they be sent on the 22nd of October to Rama and report to Siljeg and Bozo Curcija and that they would be given instructions about what they were to do. That's it. I don't need to add anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about that piece that is handwritten down at the bottom, the writing there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is Siljeg's handwriting, I believe, probably Siljeg's. And he says that part of the men have arrived and that he is faced with the problem of them not wanting to take up their positions up at the defence lines. So he's asking what to do about these people who don't want to man the lines. And what can you do? If you put him in prison, he's better off in prison than he is up at the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, which is P05560, dated the 4th of November, 1993. It is an order, your order. At least it's your signature there. We've already dealt with this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have. It's the duty operations team for the 11th of November, the commander, the deputy commander, and the other officers in the team. It's the classical type of organisational setup in the Main Staff. And at the time, the BH Army offensive had already become less intense, so we could deal with the organisational problems. And that's what we did, and that's what we have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now we come to 3D03047, the next document. You signed that document, too.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What number was that, 03047?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It is the 6th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. On the 6th of November, my signature there. This was September to Blaskic, Kordic, and Zeko. Well, their reports were becoming more and more panicked. They would write in haste, especially after the fall of Vares. And I'm telling them that Vares fell because they didn't prepare for battle properly because there was lack of organisation. They thought nobody would attack them. They were on good terms with the 3rd Corps because they supplied the 3rd Corps with everything it needed. There was a lot of black-marketeering, and then rumours were going around that somebody would be leaving Central Bosnia. And so here I'm telling them to persevere, that it is difficult, but that there is hope. Well, it's a classical letter of encouragement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what conflicts did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the BH Army attacks in Central Bosnia because the conflicts were very intensive still there and had serious repercussions. There were a lot of wounded, and the other population suffered.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now look at the next document, which is P06482.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I might come back to this document later, and I can, but I thought that while we're on it, can I ask for a clarification and make sure the translation is correct? I'm looking at the sentence there that says: "Low-spirited people to be eliminated," and I want to make sure that that is a correct translation from the original language of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Eliminate" in the Croatian language, or at least how I use it here, means to get them away from their posts, positions. Now, I don't know, in English, whether to eliminate means to deprive of life, to kill. But the way I use it in Croatian, that's what I meant, to remove them from those -- the positions, to replace them, have them replaced from their positions, to prevent them from disseminating rumours. To eliminate the problem means to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, it does not mean physically eliminate, meaning killing somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To eliminate a problem, Your Honour, means -- well, I don't know. It's a very clear word, at least in the language that I use. Whether it's a problem or -- well, you can also use a different word. I could have written "replace him," but "eliminate the problem" is short and to the point. Prevent them, incarcerate them, do whatever you like, just don't let panic overtake you because they had already started to panic. They had a lot of reason to be gravely concerned, but I say, No, that's not how you should be doing things.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you didn't answer -- you haven't answered Judge Antonetti's question. Does "to eliminate" mean to kill?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next document, which is P06482. The document is dated the 6th of November.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. That's a meeting that I convened with the commanders of two operation zones that were over there, the brigades and the commanders of the professional units. And I say that the meeting will be held on the 7th of November at 1800 hours in Tomislavgrad, and that I am asking them to attend the meeting. I was already leaving, but that didn't prevent me from completing my task. And the amount of problems that commanders from all levels put forward was such -- the problems were so great, they had so many problems, and they wanted to explain the situation precisely and clearly and state what needed to be changed for the military establishment of the army to be raised at a higher level so that they could manage their troops and the army. And that's the problem that I tried to explain to you, although I don't have a lot of time. I used the example of, well, the beginning of sociology, why Napoleon was victorious, a well-ordered army, and how the social circumstances and situation affected an army because an army is not a separate part of society. It lives with the entire political-social situation in organisational terms and so on and so forth. Anyway, this meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we please move on to 3D02029. Another one of yours.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the 8th of November, the last evening. I think on that day when I arrived, and I arrived late - I remember that well - late that evening I arrived at the Main Staff because that afternoon I had stayed until late with Mr. Roso, who was to replace me the following morning. I was trying to explain to him what the situation was. I think I signed this document and another one on behalf of Mr. Petkovic to step up the procedure about the investigation in Stupni Do. Here I signed the commission for SpaBat to carry the wounded across. I asked that in addition to Ms. Dzenija Orucevic, and her mother, Edina Orucevic, two Bosnian Muslim ladies, Josip Kordic, a Croat, also be taken, who had been wounded by a shell, and this is about the eastern side, to Mostar Hospital, and if needed, taken even further than that. I said that they should be given any assistance required. For the first time here, I ask that a Croat be taken along, too, because there had been justified complaints that had been reaching me that we were taking better care of the BH Army, for humanitarian and other reasons, than of our own people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we please go to 3D00951. The date is the 9th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, late that evening, following this meeting that I had on the 7th, I slept there and I did not go to the Main Staff the morning of the 8th; rather, I waited to meet Mr. Roso first. This happened in Livno and Tomislavgrad. We toured that part over there, and then late that evening, I was back. The morning of the 9th, at 7.35 a.m., I handed over to General Roso. He then wrote an order to the effect that at noon the same day, he would be meeting the brigade commanders in Prozor. I state that just to confirm he wouldn't have made it any other way, just to remove any doubt at all that I did, in fact, hand over to General Roso on the 9th of November, 1993, at 7.35 a.m. General Roso issued an order immediately, and he was off to war. It would have taken him at least three hours to reach Rama.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D00953, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, one question to this order. Who are the chiefs of service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, an army has different services. I'm not sure who exactly he had in mind, but he probably meant the artillery, the infantry, the signals, an army's components, individual components, and then the chiefs of these components. Whether he meant the chiefs from the Main Staff, it's probably for the chiefs of the Main Staff, the chiefs of these separate components or services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have to perhaps speculate because it's not you who wrote this order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we now please go to 3D00953, which is dated the 9th of November, 1993. You didn't produce this document. It was produced by Colonel-General Ante Roso. Can you tell us what this order says? Had General Roso taken over by this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hand-over occurred on the 9th of May [as interpreted], so he took over. This order is of no interest to me in that respect. I just wanted to ascertain the time I handed over my command duties. The only thing that is noteworthy here is paragraph 2, where he says that he will take these brigades to put together five and a half thousand soldiers. Quite obviously, Mr. Roso, who had served with the foreign legion as well for a long time, was thinking that the manpower levels in the brigades were kept up under a different system, the system that he was used to, but this figure makes no sense at all. He was later bitterly disappointed when he realised how many men were actually available to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the transcript states that the hand-over took place on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th of November, 1993, at 7.35 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I had to ask because that's what the transcript states. Can you now please go to 3D00969. The 31st of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's one of my documents. It's about the cease-fire. It was dispatched to SpaBat in Medjugorje. Again, we are asserting that we are ready to cease all hostilities in Mostar for the duration of the Medjugorje talks. The talks were happening under the chairmanship of General Felin, and the talks took place between the two armies, the Croat and the Muslim armies. And I said that SpaBat and the UN observers should oversee the cessation of hostilities on both sides. Ms. Nika, Your Honours, the recurring problem was always the fact that all sorts of things were being signed all the time in offices all over the world. But no one ever gave us a recipe as to how these things should be implemented and under whose supervision. Each time, whenever we signed something, we asked. Please, look at page 3. EU observers or UNPROFOR, may they oversee both sides, supervise both sides, just to make sure we know who it is that is violating the cease-fire? But, no, the cease-fire is signed. No one was prepared to supervise its implementation. Everyone was off to a more leisurely life somewhere else, to put it that way. And then after that, obviously, the BH Army claimed that it was us violating the cease-fire, and we were saying that they were attacking us. The fighting was becoming fiercer and fiercer, and then the observers would check god-knows-what information, who started first. They were probably under some political instructions or other. Each of the documents said, Now that you have recognised the Republic of Croatia, place along its borders small military contingents of your own to make sure that the cease-fires are upheld. The UN mandate did not allow for that, and maybe no one was interested, as simple as that, but we never managed to achieve any degree of control in terms of any of the cease-fires signed being implemented equally on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about the 31st of August; was there a cease-fire that took effect on the 31st of August? Can you still remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so, for a while at least. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: At the time, do you remember what was going on in Mostar? Let me prompt you. There was a humanitarian convoy on its way in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, you don't remember then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember one on the 25th. I was involved, and then later, other convoys came. There were convoys on their way and all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I didn't mean the convoy, but the circumstances. But it doesn't really matter. We're done with the Main Staff now and are about to move on to a file entitled "Effective Control."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in the binder. It's like this [indicates]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to understand things clearly, Ms. Pinter, is this your last binder or will there be other binders after this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a little more. We have Mostar-93, several documents from Mostar in relation to the snipers and the Old Bridge. We also have a number of questions left. We have two books, and we have another binder that is important. This one has been handed over to you, and we informed our learned friend, Mr. Stringer. These are documents that require some explanations, and the general will try and shed some light on these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I put the question to you because I was trying to understand how much time you needed still. You've had an hour and 30 minutes more. We will most probably be sitting on Monday as well, since as things stand, we will run on until the end, until Monday, then we will have a break for the week. And when Mr. Stringer comes back, we will resume on the following Monday.
